A brooch is a decorative ornament — a piece of jewellery — that you attach directly to your clothing.

A brooch is typically a small, flat or slightly three-dimensional object, usually no bigger than your palm. It can take almost any shape: a flower, a butterfly, a leaf, an animal, a geometric pattern, an abstract design, or even a portrait. It can be plain and simple, or it can be richly detailed and studded with gemstones, pearls, or colourful enamel.

The materials vary widely. Brooches can be made of gold, silver, bronze, or other metals; they can feature diamonds, rubies, sapphires, or other precious and semi-precious stones; they can be made of glass, plastic, fabric, wood, or even painted porcelain. In short, a brooch can range from a cheap, everyday trinket to an extraordinarily valuable and historic piece of fine jewellery.
The defining feature: the pin and clasp on the back

What makes a brooch a brooch — and sets it apart from other decorative objects — is its attachment mechanism. On the back of every brooch, there is a small, sharp metal pin (like a long thin needle) along with a small locking clasp or catch. To wear a brooch, you push the pin through the fabric of your garment and then click it securely into the catch. This holds the brooch firmly in place without damaging the clothing beyond a very small, nearly invisible hole.

This pin-and-clasp system is the essential, defining characteristic of a brooch. If an ornament doesn't have this mechanism, it is generally not called a brooch.

A brooch is worn on the outside of clothing — never underneath. The most common placements are:

  • On the chest or bust area, slightly to one side
  • On a lapel (the folded-back flap on a jacket or coat)
  • At the collar or neckline
  • On a hat, beret, or headband
  • On a scarf, shawl, or sash — sometimes to gather and hold the fabric elegantly in place
  • On a belt or handbag

The chest and lapel are by far the most traditional and common locations.
What a brooch is used for

A brooch serves two purposes, and these often overlap:

1. Pure decoration. Most of the time, a brooch is simply worn because it looks beautiful or meaningful. It adds a focal point, a splash of colour, or a personal statement to an outfit. A plain black jacket can be transformed by a single striking brooch at the lapel.

2. Functional fastening. Historically — and still sometimes today — brooches were used to actually hold garments together. Imagine a large draped shawl that keeps slipping open: a brooch pinned through the overlapping layers holds everything in place neatly. Ancient peoples used large brooches (called fibulae) to fasten robes and cloaks the same way we use buttons today.

In modern usage, the decorative purpose is dominant, but the functional aspect is never entirely gone.
How a brooch differs from similar things

It helps to distinguish a brooch from a few closely related items:

  • A pin (like a lapel pin or enamel pin): Much simpler and usually smaller. A pin typically has a single post or wire on the back rather than a full pin-and-clasp mechanism. The word "pin" is often used casually and loosely, but a brooch is the grander, more elaborate, more jewellery-like version.
  • A badge: Usually carries text, a logo, or a symbol identifying affiliation (a school badge, a name tag, a campaign button). Functional and institutional in character, not primarily jewellery. It uses a similar pin mechanism, but the intent and aesthetic are entirely different.
  • A clip: Some ornaments attach to clothing using a pressure clip rather than a pin that pierces the fabric. These are sometimes called "clip brooches" or "dress clips." The mechanism is different, but the decorative intent is the same.

Historically, both men and women wore brooches — they were practical fasteners for everyone. Over the centuries, they became more associated with women's fashion, where they remain a classic jewellery staple. Today, men also wear them, particularly on suit lapels, and in many cultures brooches are a genderless accessory.

Brooches have been worn by royalty and ordinary people alike. Queen Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom was famously known for her extraordinary collection of brooches, which she wore at nearly every public appearance — and which she often chose deliberately to send subtle messages or honour occasions.

You might encounter brooches:

  • In a jewellery shop, displayed alongside rings, necklaces, and earrings
  • Pinned to the lapel of an older relative's coat
  • As a gift item — a sentimental or heirloom piece passed down through generations
  • In antique markets, where vintage and antique brooches are highly collectible
  • On formal or ceremonial occasions, where they add elegance to an outfit
The core idea, in one sentence

A brooch is a decorative jewellery piece that fastens to clothing via a pin-and-clasp on its back, worn primarily for beauty, occasionally for function, and almost always as a personal or stylistic statement.
